newsitem.title: USA: Semiconductor CEOs to discuss trade issues at Hawaii summit.
newsitem.headline: Semiconductor CEOs to discuss trade issues at Hawaii summit.

text.p: Chief executives of American, Japanese and European computer chip makers planned to meet in Hawaii over the weekend to discuss ways to open Japanese markets further for semiconductor imports.

The CEOs will convene at the first meeting of the Semiconductor Council, a worldwide industry organisation set up last summer to help international semiconductor companies resolve trade issues without government intervention.
American executives will ask their Japanese counterparts to continue their volunteer efforts to buy more computer chips from the U.S. and abroad, industry representatives said.

"The purpose of all this is to open markets," said Daryl Hatano, acting president of the Semiconductor Industry Association, which represents the interests of U.S. chip makers. "The way to encourage the industry to grow is through open markets."

U.S. and Japanese executives set up the Semiconductor Council in August, when a trade agreement between the countries expired. The executives failed to set up a new formal trade agreement, but agreed to form a worldwide trade body to hash out differences.

Japanese and American semiconductor industries have had a contentious past. During much of the 1980s, U.S. and foreign chip supplies accounted for less than 10 percent of semiconductor sales in Japan, even though the U.S. is practically the only source for microprocessors, the brains of personal computers.

In 1986, Under pressure from President Ronald Reagan's administration, the Japanese signed a six-year agreement to increase the share of foreign suppliers to 20 percent by 1991. By that year, the foreign share was still just 14 percent, so the countries drew up another agreement aiming for 20 percent by 1996.

The Japanese met the goal. By the third quarter of 1996, 27 percent of semiconductor sales in Japan were to foreign suppliers, according to the SIA. So Japanese trade representatives argued at a Vancouver conference in August that there was no need for another agreement.
At the Semiconductor Council meeting this weekend, U.S. executives will ask Japan to improve foreign access to the Japanese market, association officials said.
On the agenda is discussions to figure out how the council can collect market share data in Japan to gauge the effectiveness of the voluntary agreements.

Meanwhile, executives of European and Korean chipmakers will seek to join the council, in hopes of increasing their access to Japanese markets, SIA officials said. As part of the requirement to join the council, Korea and Europe earlier this year agreed to eliminate semiconductor tariffs on chips entering their markets by the end of the decade.
Executives also planned to discuss cooperation on research projects and ways to reduce toxic waste produced by the industry.
